parakeet: Carl Sagan warned about this exact problem in the demon haunted world. He pointed out something that still haunts me to this day. We live in a society completely dependent on science and technology, yet almost nobody understands how any of it actually works. We know how to turn things on, but we don't know how things work. We are a society that knows how to turn the lights on, but has no idea how the grid functions. We have strong opinions about economies and yet have never studied economics. And that gap creates a dangerous illusion. We think we know more than we actually do. This leads to something I call cognitive lethargy. People fall in love with ideas, but they never test them. They mistake having an idea for having a solution. You see it everywhere. Political theories, economic ideas, even cultural movements and social media debates. Everyone has a plan for the world, but very few people are actually experimenting with their ideas. It's easier to fall in love with a grand sweeping vision than it is to do the embarrassingly grunt work of a pilot program. Here's the reality: an idea is not a plan. A plan is not a solution, and a solution is not real until it survives experimentation. A real solution is something that has been tested, executed, refined, and proven to work. So personally, I've developed a filter. I don't want to hear your big ideas if you're not experimenting with them. I don't want to hear your solutions if you've never executed them. To me, this is the basis of modern superstition. Loving an idea simply because it's yours, not because it's proven. And when someone speaks with absolute certainty but has zero experimentation and zero execution, I know something immediately. They're still thinking like a believer.
